extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of folklore/ethnography; general readers interested in popular superstition
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive/analytic account of folk practices (charms, amulets, incantations) and beliefs about the luck of numbers, with examples and local variants from many countries and epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and occasion-specific performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Charms and anti-animal rites are frequently required to be performed at particular times or on special days (e.g., Christmas Eve, the first holiday of the year, Good Friday morning, Easter Sunday, the last day of February, dawn of a principal feast day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "On Christmas Eve ... the following sentence is repeated: 'O mice, eat these remnants and leave the grain in peace!'"; Thuringian rats-clearing done "Before sunrise on Good Friday morning"; Bulgarian women beat copper vessels "on the last day of February." The account implies timing is an essential component of efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of food offerings and harvest-procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving or scattering food or parts of the harvest (leftover meal, last sheaf, blessed loaves, loaves buried or thrown into fields) as a propitiatory or protective act against vermin or locusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peas thrown on barn floor at Christmas; "the last sheaf of corn is left standing" and surrounded with a hymn; Spanish farmers carried "loaves of bread to be blessed" and then buried or threw them into cornfields to protect crops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific plants, herbs, and botanical amulets
rubrics_metrics.description: Carrying or placing particular herbs/plants (periwinkle/Vinca, Anchusa officinalis/bugloss, mountain ash/rowan, Dracontium, Myosotis) as charms to guard against snakes, vipers, wild animals, or as talismans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pliny's recommended herb (bugloss) as amulet; Anglo-Saxons carried periwinkle as charm against snakes; rowan branches twined about cattle horns to avert witches; Doctrine of Signatures used plant resemblance (e.g., Dracontium 'great dragon') as rationale for efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images/figures and homœopathic principle ('like cures like')
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing images or figures of animals to either repel or attract creatures, based on the homœopathic idea that 'Like cures like.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hanging a dead crow in a cornfield to protect crops; painting a half crow on cloth and burying it to attract crows; brazen images (scorpion, serpent, dormouse) used as talismans protecting cities—explicitly tied to the homœopathic doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal charms, incantations, and formulae (including unintelligibility and repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of specific sentences, prayers, or magical formulas is central; potency often ascribed to the words themselves (sometimes their unintelligibility), with repetition (often three times) common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Catholic formulas against vipers reproduced in full; incantations repeated thrice (e.g., a French fox-charm "to be repeated thrice a week"); medieval cabalists valued unintelligible charm-words. Many local chants and verses are quoted as complete recipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of noise, processional acts, and movement-based rituals
rubrics_metrics.description: Making noise or staging processions (trumpets, instruments, jingling keys, beating copper vessels, mock funerals) to frighten or symbolically destroy pests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mixco farmers assembled with trumpets to scare locusts; Bechlin peasant rattles keys while church-bells ring to drive away mice; Bulgarian women beat copper vessels shouting to frighten snakes and scorpions; Albanian women form a mock funeral procession for locusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material-object rituals and directional/place prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and placement of particular objects (old unclean shoe at a crossroads, inked mice on maps, knife stuck where insects congregate) and prescribed directions or dispositions as part of the charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laying an old shoe at a crossroads and silently repeating a Paternoster to determine flight direction of rats; mice with inked feet placed on map to 'foretell' routes; black-handled knife stuck where insects gather while verses are recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astrological timing and preparation of talismans
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting astrological 'proper time' for burying or activating images/talismans and preparing items (engraving, engraving figures on metal) with attention to planetary or astrological determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Antoine Mizauld's prescription that to drive away serpents one should engrave two serpents on copper and pronounce a charm "at the proper time, as determined by astrology."

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious sanction, exorcism, and ecclesiastical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking or employing church-sanctioned rites (blessings, excommunications, prayers, sanctioned formulas) and invoking saints or sacred names as part of charms and expulsions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "The Roman Catholic Church formerly sanctioned the use of certain sentences as charms against vipers"; monks scattering blessed crumbs to repel vermin; invocation of saints (St. Nicholas Tolentine) and use of relics; Ritual of Séez forbade such practices without special permission, showing ecclesiastical regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-first principle (natural measures before supernatural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation (by authorities like Pierre Le Brun) that mundane, practical measures (open the door, use a stick, throw food out) should precede prayer or supernatural expedients; supernatural means reserved if practical steps fail and ideally with ecclesiastical sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted counsel: do not begin with prayer and holy water when driving out a strange dog—first try pragmatic actions. This is presented as a rational anti-superstitious guideline within the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and communal remedies against pests (prosecution and ritualized justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities historically instituted legal proceedings against animals (prosecutions, appointed counsel, sentencing, excommunication) and ritualized communal remedies as an officially recognized response to depredations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trials of rats, bulls, pigs, locusts in France/Switzerland/Spain; practice of appointing counsel and prosecuting attorney for animal 'defendants'; the deodand doctrine (forfeiture of chattel causing death) as legal relic. Described as a customary/legal remedy rather than magical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Signatures and physical resemblance reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that a plant's external appearance indicates therapeutic or protective virtue (e.g., plants resembling serpents or scorpions used as antidotes against those creatures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dracontium ('great dragon') thought preservative against serpents; scorpion-grass (Myosotis) thought antidote to scorpion sting. Herbalists claimed plants could drive away wolves, leopards, and venomous beasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and valorization of odd numbers (three, seven, nine) in charms and architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Odd numbers—especially three, seven, and nine—are repeatedly regarded as auspicious and are systematically employed in rituals, incantations, architecture, and ceremonial counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chinese pagodas built with odd number of stories; Siamese houses required odd numbers of rooms/doors/steps; witches' incantations favoring multiples of three; many ethnographic examples and mythic associations (seven planets, seven heavens) offered as rationale.
